1	# Issue #230: a browser page on the remote port, investigation notes
2	
3	Read: CLAUDE.md, docs/lessons.md (84 lines, nothing about the remote port;
4	its lesson is the action/effect core, a fake for every port, and "spike
5	risky technology first"), docs/remote-client.md §§0–5, design.md "Trust
6	boundary" (l.219) and the start of "Remote client (2026-10-12)" (l.3107),
7	plus the code below. Line numbers are as they are in this worktree at
8	7fe8949. There is no `web/` directory yet.
9	
10	## The record first: what is on disk, and how it comes back
11	
12	- **No new record kind and no `model.rs` change is needed.** A browser is
13	  one more `PairedDevice` (`src/ports/remote.rs:96-107`: `id`, `name`,
14	  `scope`, `token_sha256`, `created`, `last_seen`) in
15	  `<data dir>/devices.json`. That file is a bare `Vec<PairedDevice>`
16	  with no schema version (`RemoteFiles::load_devices`/`save_devices`,
17	  `src/adapters/remote.rs:80-86`), written atomically by
18	  `Effect::SaveDevices` (`src/core/remote.rs:121-125`). The name comes
19	  from `/pair`'s `device_name` (`src/app.rs:3650-3655`), cut to 64 chars
20	  in `AppCore::new_device` (`src/core/remote.rs:166-175`). So "Safari on
21	  iPhone" can be the page's own `device_name` with no host change. If
22	  the plan wants a `kind` (browser or native) on the device, it is an
23	  additive `#[serde(default)]` field in a file that has no version.
24	- **Rehydration** is unchanged: `IdentityLoaded { identity, devices,
25	  rotated }` (`src/core/remote.rs:22-30`) puts the devices back at
26	  launch. A token is checked by hash against them on every request
27	  (`authenticate`, `src/app.rs:3125-3153`; `device_by_token`,
28	  `src/core/remote.rs:145-147`). Revoke (`RevokeDevice`,
29	  `src/core/remote.rs:86-92`) and scope change (`:93-100`) apply on the
30	  next request, and revoke closes the device's socket (test
31	  `revoke_closes_the_devices_socket`, `tests/remote.rs:2892`).
32	- **The pairing window is not durable** (`PairingWindow` in core state:
33	  code, scope, `until`, failures; `OpenPairing`/`ClosePairing`/
34	  `PairingFailed`/`Paired`, `src/core/remote.rs:46-73`). The QR is built
35	  in the UI from it (`src/ui/remote.rs:155-173`). Changing JSON to a URL
36	  is a change to that `json!` call and to the "Copy invite" text (`:199-206`),
37	  not to any record.
38	- **The page itself is not a record.** It is static bytes compiled in
39	  (`include_str!`). On the device, what persists is the token, plus
40	  whatever the page keeps to say "identity changed". Decision 2 picks
41	  where that is. The browser also keeps its certificate exception per
42	  host. The host keeps nothing new per browser beyond the device record.
43	- **Identity** (`identity.json`, `Identity` at `src/ports/remote.rs:26-42`,
44	  `IDENTITY_SCHEMA_VERSION = 1` at `:17`). It holds the certificate
45	  (base64 DER) and `spki_sha256`. The certificate is made by
46	  `make_identity` (`src/adapters/remote.rs:95-127`) with
47	  `CertificateParams::new(Vec::<String>::new())`: **no subjectAltName at
48	  all**, a CN of `Switchboard <server_id>`, rcgen's default validity
49	  (the comment says `not_after` is the year 4096), and no EKU set
50	  explicitly. The native clients pin the SPKI and ignore names, so this
51	  never mattered. A browser checks names and validity. Changing the
52	  certificate (adding SANs for the LAN address or a `.local` name, or a
53	  bounded validity) changes nothing the pin sees if the key is reused
54	  (the SPKI is the same, §5). But the certificate is stored in
55	  `identity.json`, so reissuing it means writing that file, and an
56	  address that moves would need another reissue.

58	## What the code does today, piece by piece
59	
60	### The listener (`src/adapters/remote.rs`)
61	
62	- `read_request` (`:444-513`) keeps the method, the path, the query
63	  (undecoded), the body, `bearer` (`Authorization: Bearer`, `:487-491`)
64	  and `upgrade` (`Sec-WebSocket-Key` when `Upgrade: websocket`,
65	  `:492-495`). It throws away every other header. **It does not read
66	  `Cookie`, `Origin`, `User-Agent`, `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol`, `Host`,
67	  `If-None-Match` or `Accept`.** Either token transport in decision 2
68	  needs a new `RemoteRequest` field. That struct is in
69	  `src/adapters/remote.rs:359-372`, which is not under `ports/`, but
70	  `tests/remote.rs` builds requests and should be checked.
71	- `respond` (`:530-552`) always writes `Content-Type: application/json`
72	  and `Connection: keep-alive`, nothing else. It has no CSP, no
73	  Cache-Control, no Set-Cookie and no other content type. `RemoteReply`
74	  (`:388-393`) is `{status, body, authenticated}`. Static files and a
75	  cookie on `/pair` therefore need `RemoteReply` (or a separate
76	  connection-thread path) to carry headers. `respond_upgrade`
77	  (`:519-527`) writes no `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol`. A browser that offered
78	  a subprotocol fails the handshake if the server does not echo one
79	  (that is a question below, not checked).
80	- Pools and windows: `MAX_UNAUTHENTICATED = 4`, `MAX_PAIRED = 12`
81	  (`:567-568`). A stream past the 4 is dropped at accept (`:699-706`). A
82	  connection moves pools only when a reply says `authenticated: true`
83	  (`:834-849`). `HANDSHAKE_TIMEOUT` is 5 s (`:570`), and the first
84	  request line has the same deadline. `IDLE_TIMEOUT` is 30 s (`:573`).
85	  The rate windows exist only for `/api/v1/pair` (6/min) and
86	  `/api/v1/info` (60/min) (`:583-587`, `Limits::limited` `:629-640`).
87	  Any other path, a static one included, is unlimited and goes to the
88	  frame. What this means for a page load: a browser opens several
89	  parallel connections and keeps them alive. Static GETs leave a
90	  connection in the unauthenticated pool for up to 30 s idle. A
91	  failed TLS handshake (the certificate warning) also holds a slot until
92	  it ends. **The pool of 4 is what an unpaired page load competes for.**
93	  Once paired, each fetch with the cookie or token moves its connection
94	  to the paired pool. The test `stalled_strangers_fill_their_own_pool_and_never_a_paired_clients`
95	  (`tests/remote.rs:3226`) is the existing model for that behaviour.
96	- The frame drain: `port.poll(DRAIN_PER_PASS)` then `serve_remote` for
97	  each (`src/app.rs:1585-1597`). The connection thread answers 429/503/504
98	  without the frame (`src/adapters/remote.rs:787-833`). Static bytes
99	  could be answered on the connection thread the same way (they need no
100	  core state), or on the frame through `serve_remote`. §4.1 "the frame
101	  does core state only" leans toward the connection thread. Not decided
102	  here.
103	
104	### The router (`src/app.rs`)
105	
106	- `serve_remote` (`:3017-3121`) refuses any path without the `/api/v1/`
107	  prefix with 404 `not_found` (`:3023-3025`). Then it answers `info` and
108	  `pair` unauthenticated (`:3027-3031`), authenticates, and handles
109	  `events` (`:3036-3038`) and the allowlist. The static paths would be a
110	  new arm before the prefix match, and they are the third thing served
111	  before pairing (§5's rule, `docs/remote-client.md` l.390 in the
112	  section, "Require pairing before anything but `/info` and `/pair`").
113	- `authenticate` (`:3125-3153`) knows only `request.bearer`. Both its
114	  refusals have the code `unauthorized`, with different messages: "pair
115	  this device first" (no token) and "the token is not known; pair again"
116	  (revoked, rotated, or never valid). **A page cannot tell "revoked"
117	  from "never paired" by the code.** With an HttpOnly cookie, the page
118	  cannot even see whether it holds a token. The "revoked" state in the
119	  issue needs either a distinct code (additive) or a non-secret marker
120	  the page keeps itself (for example, "I paired with server X as device
121	  Y").
122	- `remote_subscribe` (`:2723-2758`) requires `request.upgrade` and a
123	  device. It does not check `Origin`. Neither does anything else.
124	- `remote_pair` (`:3606-3674`) compares the body's `spki_sha256` with the
125	  host's own, then the code, uppercased. It counts a failure on either
126	  (`PairingFailed`). It answers `{token, scope, server_id, device_id}` in
127	  the envelope. A cookie would be set here.
128	- `remote_info` (`:3568-3600`) carries `spki_sha256`, `server_name`,
129	  `capabilities`, `version`, `pairing_open`, but not the device's scope
130	  (it is unauthenticated). The header's "scope" comes from the `/pair`
131	  reply, and after that from nowhere: **no endpoint today tells a device
132	  its current scope**. A scope change in the dialog is invisible until a
133	  `control` command is refused. The Swift client has the same gap.
134	- `refuse` (`:3754-3772`) logs method and path, never the query. A
135	  `GET /?code=…` that reached the router would not log the code. Any
136	  new static handler must keep that true.

207	## Things the issue asserts that the tree contradicts or leaves open
208	
209	- "Any path outside `/api/v1/` is refused": true (`src/app.rs:3023`), but
210	  on the frame, after the request was queued (so it costs inbox space),
211	  not at the connection thread.
212	- "the one-line excerpt the card shows" is not on the wire (above).
213	- "the device's scope in the header": no endpoint returns it after
214	  pairing (above).
215	- "'revoked' said plainly": the refusal code does not distinguish it
216	  (above).
217	- The `key` check in the page compares the URL's key with what `/info`
218	  says. A page cannot read the TLS certificate it is talking over, so
219	  this proves only that the host *claims* that key. A relay forwards
220	  `/info` faithfully, and the host's own `spki_sha256` check in
221	  `remote_pair` (`:3639-3647`) is fed by the page's body, which is the
222	  impostor's page under a relay. What it does catch is a genuine page on
223	  the wrong genuine host (a second installation at that address or
224	  port, or a rotated key). The issue says roughly this. The tree adds
225	  that §5's sentence "the host refuses a pairing whose `spki_sha256` is
226	  not its own, so a relayed request … fails" does not hold for a
227	  browser, and the spec text must say so.
228	- Cookies are scoped by host, not by port. Two Switchboard instances on
229	  one Mac (`SWITCHBOARD_REMOTE_PORT`, design §3.1) and any other HTTPS
230	  service on another port of that host would all receive a
231	  `Secure` cookie set by one of them. A cookie name per `server_id`
232	  avoids the clash between instances. It does not stop another service
233	  on that host from receiving it. `localStorage` is per origin
234	  (scheme, host and port), so it does not have this problem, but any
235	  script on the origin can read it.

8	
9	- `new WebSocket(url, protocols)` takes no headers. WHATWG, https://websockets.spec.whatwg.org/ (fetched); MDN WebSocket (fetched). Q3, Q6.
10	- The server may send `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` only with a value derived from the client's offer, and must not send it otherwise. If protocols were offered and none comes back, the browser fails the connection. RFC 6455 §4.2.2, https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6455 (fetched); WHATWG (fetched). So a token carrier needs the server to echo one offered value.
11	- Subprotocol values are `1#token`, U+0021–U+007E, unique; a violation throws SyntaxError. RFC 6455 §4.1 (fetched); MDN (fetched).
12	- The server "SHOULD verify the Origin field" and "SHOULD respond … 403" if unexpected. RFC 6455 §10.2 (fetched, offset 100000). The allowlist is the owner's.
13	- Cookies "do not provide isolation by port". RFC 6265 §8.5, https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6265 (fetched). `__Host-` does not change this.
14	- `Secure` limits a cookie to secure channels (RFC 6265 §4.1.2.5, fetched). `__Host-` needs `Secure`, a secure page, no `Domain`, `Path=/`. MDN Cookies guide, https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/Cookies (fetched). Vendor docs, no contradiction.
15	- `SameSite=Strict` cookies are sent "only in response to requests originating from the cookie's origin site." Same MDN page. WebSocket is not named (Unresolved).
16	- An `https` or `wss` origin is potentially trustworthy by scheme alone; certificate validity is not a condition. W3C Secure Contexts §3.1 step 3, https://www.w3.org/TR/secure-contexts/ (fetched). The search's claim that a certificate-error page "is generally not a secure context" is unsourced; do not build on it. Q5.

524:## 13. Explicit design decisions
The files of each attempt (2026-10-18) ride on the single-ticket read: `TicketAttempt.files` names each artifact the attempt wrote (its notes, a plan, a review summary), the log of the stage's checks, each review round's findings and response, and every file of its evidence directory, with a `kind`, whether it is `inline` text or an `image`, and for evidence its size and time. A file is named by a `key`, a hash of its path, so the path stays on the Mac; a secret artifact is listed as `secret` and never read. `GET dispatch/tickets/{id}/files/{key}` answers `{key, text}` for text, through the Mac's own `DispatchReadArtifact` (so Dispatch's refusals, of a secret or of a file outside the ticket, are the device's answer, and a text the Mac already holds for the ticket as it stands is answered from its cache), bounded at 256 KiB; for an evidence image it answers `{key, media, data}` with the bytes as base64, read from the disk here, up to 700 KiB (`too_large`, 413, beyond that). `GET dispatch/tickets/{id}/events` is the ticket's event log as the Mac's cache holds it after its `DispatchReadEvents`, `{events, last, unavailable}`, served from the cache while the ticket has not changed; both reads are deferred until Dispatch answers, as the commands are. `close` is the third command, refused as `not_closable` (409) unless the status says the ticket may be closed. The attempt also carries its `checks` (head and exit) and its review `rounds`. `info` lists `evidence` for all of this, and a client shows a host without it the files by name only.

## 5. Security and pairing

A local network is not a trust boundary: these APIs can instruct coding agents and expose private transcripts. The repo's rules apply unchanged: secret values never reach a record, a log line, a command line, or any reply but `env.resolve` (which is not on this port) and, as redacted text, the read models of §4.3; the Keychain holds key material.

- Require pairing **before** anything but `/info` and `/pair`.
- **Host identity**: a self-signed certificate made once with `rcgen` on first listen. The certificate is in `identity.json` (§3.1); its private key is a Keychain item through the existing adapter (`adapters/keychain.rs`, service `com.sadburger.switchboard`) under the account `remote-key:<server_id>`, so two data directories under one macOS account never overwrite each other's keys. The bundle must be signed with the stable identity (`scripts/bundle.sh`) or the Keychain ACL is lost on every rebuild.
- **What the client pins** is the SPKI SHA-256 of the host's public key, not the certificate's bytes, so a certificate reissued from the same key (a new expiry) still verifies. Rotating the key is making a new identity: every pairing is invalid and the dialog says so.
- **Pairing verifies the key before the code is sent.** The code alone would let an intermediary terminate the first connection, forward the code to the real host, and take the token. So the pairing window shows a **QR code** carrying `{server_id, spki_sha256, code, addresses}`, and under it the same in text: a short form of the key hash and the code. The client scans or types both; it connects, compares the hash of the key it is actually talking to with the one it was given, and only when they match sends `/pair {code, device_name, spki_sha256}`. A client without a camera (visionOS gives an app none) pairs from the host's Bonjour record instead: it resolves the record, reads `/info` under no trust, shows the key the host presented in the dialog's short form for the owner to compare by eye, and pins that key for the pairing, so the typed code reaches only the host whose key the owner checked; a substituted certificate shows its own key on the device, where the owner sees it differ. The host refuses a pairing whose `spki_sha256` is not its own, so a relayed request through a substituted certificate fails even if the code reached it. Before pairing, `/info` is served to any client and nothing in it is trusted; after pairing, every connection verifies the pin before the token is presented.
- The pairing window is opened from the settings menu as "Allow pairing for 5 minutes", the same shape as the environment setup window (`ENV_SETUP_WINDOW`, never saved). The dialog that opens it chooses the scope the pairing grants, `read` by default.
- **The code**: eight characters from the 32-character Crockford alphabet (no `I`, `L`, `O`, `U`), 40 bits, drawn from the OS random source (`getrandom`), made when the window opens and shown as the QR's `code` and in text. It is single-use: the first successful `/pair` consumes it and closes the window. **Failures count globally**: one counter in the app's state, bumped on the frame for every failed `/pair` from any connection, and the window closes at three. Concurrent attempts cannot each get three, because the frame answers them in arrival order against the one counter.
- **The token**: 32 bytes from the OS random source, base64url, 43 characters. It does not expire; the owner revokes. It is sent only as a bearer header over the pinned connection, never in a URL.
- `/pair` answers with the token and the granted scope. The host stores the device name, scope, created time, last-seen time and the token's SHA-256 in `<data dir>/devices.json` (atomic write, owner-readable); never the token. The client stores the token and the pinned key hash in its Keychain.
- **Scope changes** happen in the host's dialog: a device's scope can be raised to `control` or lowered to `read` there, taking effect on the device's next request. There is no scope request over the port.
- **Key rotation** (a missing key at listen, §3.1) **deletes every record in `devices.json`** when the new identity is made, so an old token stops working on the first request, and the dialog says the pairings are gone. A client seeing a new key for a known `server_id` shows "identity changed, pair again" and sends nothing, token included.
- Every later request carries the bearer token; the host answers with the device's scope. A Settings dialog (built the way the Environment dialog is) lists paired devices with scope, last seen, and Revoke, and states what redaction does and does not cover. Revocation removes the record, takes effect on the next request and closes the device's WebSocket.

- Default view: all connected hosts, with source labels.
- Filter by server, working set, session kind, and state (`CardState` labels: waiting on you, working, idle, starting, exited, not running, not resumable).
- Sorting across hosts: the host's own rank (waiting first, then working, starting, idle, exited, not running, mirroring `CardState::rank`), then last activity, then record id as the tie-breaker.
- Server management screen: discovered and known servers, status, pairing, rename, enable/disable, forget.
- Working sets with the same name on different servers stay separate by qualified id; the UI groups by source.
- No client-made cross-host working set in v1. The host's sets are read-only from the client.

## 9. Remote access later

/// One HTTP request over a fresh pinned TLS connection: the status and
/// the body.
fn http(
    addr: SocketAddr,
    config: &Arc<ClientConfig>,
    method: &str,
    path: &str,
    bearer: Option<&str>,
    body: &str,
) -> std::io::Result<(u16, String)> {
    let tcp = TcpStream::connect(addr)?;
    tcp.set_read_timeout(Some(Duration::from_secs(10)))?;
    let conn = ClientConnection::new(
        Arc::clone(config),
        ServerName::try_from("localhost").unwrap(),
    )
    .map_err(std::io::Error::other)?;
    let mut s = StreamOwned::new(conn, tcp);
    while s.conn.is_handshaking() {
        s.conn.complete_io(&mut s.sock)?;
    }
    let auth = bearer
        .map(|t| format!("Authorization: Bearer {t}\r\n"))
        .unwrap_or_default();
    write!(
        s,
        "{method} {path} HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: localhost\r\n{auth}Content-Length: {}\r\n\r\n{body}",
        body.len()
    )?;
    s.flush()?;
    let mut reader = BufReader::new(s);
    let mut line = String::new();
    reader.read_line(&mut line)?;
    let status: u16 = line
        .split_whitespace()
        .nth(1)
        .and_then(|s| s.parse().ok())
        .ok_or_else(|| std::io::Error::new(std::io::ErrorKind::InvalidData, line.clone()))?;
    let mut length = 0usize;
    loop {
        let mut h = String::new();
        reader.read_line(&mut h)?;
        let h = h.trim_end();
        if h.is_empty() {
            break;
        }
        if let Some(v) = h.strip_prefix("Content-Length:") {
            length = v.trim().parse().unwrap_or(0);
        }
    }
    let mut out = vec![0; length];
    reader.read_exact(&mut out)?;
    Ok((status, String::from_utf8_lossy(&out).into_owned()))
}

# Changelog

Every user-visible change goes under Unreleased as it lands.
`scripts/bump.sh` moves that section under the next version with the
date, and `scripts/release.sh` publishes that section as the release
notes. The format follows [Keep a Changelog](https://keepachangelog.com)
and the versions follow [Semantic Versioning](https://semver.org).

## [Unreleased]

## [0.4.1] - 2026-10-21

- Dispatch takes an issue once per project rather than once across the data directory, so a second project on the same repository can take an issue the first already holds.

## [0.4.0] - 2026-10-21

### Added

- Dispatch reports each ticket's tokens by model and agent time, per attempt, stage and ticket, in `dispatch report` and a Usage tab on the ticket page.

### Fixed

- The session page's token count counts each message once, not once per content block, skips Claude Code's synthetic messages, and names each model when a session used more than one.

## [0.3.0] - 2026-10-19

### Added

- A session can be opened from the headset: a plus button on the Sessions tab, or "New session in this project" on a listed session, opens a Claude Code, Codex or shell session in a project on any connected host paired under the control scope, in the project's root or a directory under it, with a first message for an agent; the new session's window opens on the reply. The remote port takes `POST projects/{id}/sessions` for it and lists `create` among its capabilities.
- The remote port serves Dispatch's tickets: a listing with each ticket's standing and decisions, one ticket with its body, attempts and lanes, and under the control scope a decision answered or a parked ticket resumed. The headset gets a Tickets tab on it.
- The headset reads what each stage produced: every attempt lists its notes and other artifacts, its checks log, its review rounds' findings and responses and its evidence, each opened with a tap as text or as a picture; a ticket's timeline is read from the runner's event log; and a closable ticket can be closed. The ticket list is ordered last moved first, with a menu for the order (waiting first, newest, by project), the hosts, projects and states (closed hidden unless asked) and a "waiting on me" switch.

### Changed

- The headset's conversation view follows the end as a mode: it is held at the end, nothing growing under it can leave it behind, and a button at the right edge releases it for reading; the ellipsis at the foot returns it to following. Before, a new turn that began with a tool call could push the end off screen and switch following off, and the view could jump up to the turn it last held at the top.

### Fixed

- The headset's filter menu no longer jumps back to its top every couple of seconds while open: it is rebuilt only when a host or a session state it lists changes, not on every refresh.

524:## 13. Explicit design decisions
The files of each attempt (2026-10-18) ride on the single-ticket read: `TicketAttempt.files` names each artifact the attempt wrote (its notes, a plan, a review summary), the log of the stage's checks, each review round's findings and response, and every file of its evidence directory, with a `kind`, whether it is `inline` text or an `image`, and for evidence its size and time. A file is named by a `key`, a hash of its path, so the path stays on the Mac; a secret artifact is listed as `secret` and never read. `GET dispatch/tickets/{id}/files/{key}` answers `{key, text}` for text, through the Mac's own `DispatchReadArtifact` (so Dispatch's refusals, of a secret or of a file outside the ticket, are the device's answer, and a text the Mac already holds for the ticket as it stands is answered from its cache), bounded at 256 KiB; for an evidence image it answers `{key, media, data}` with the bytes as base64, read from the disk here, up to 700 KiB (`too_large`, 413, beyond that). `GET dispatch/tickets/{id}/events` is the ticket's event log as the Mac's cache holds it after its `DispatchReadEvents`, `{events, last, unavailable}`, served from the cache while the ticket has not changed; both reads are deferred until Dispatch answers, as the commands are. `close` is the third command, refused as `not_closable` (409) unless the status says the ticket may be closed. The attempt also carries its `checks` (head and exit) and its review `rounds`. `info` lists `evidence` for all of this, and a client shows a host without it the files by name only.

## 5. Security and pairing

A local network is not a trust boundary: these APIs can instruct coding agents and expose private transcripts. The repo's rules apply unchanged: secret values never reach a record, a log line, a command line, or any reply but `env.resolve` (which is not on this port) and, as redacted text, the read models of §4.3; the Keychain holds key material.

- Require pairing **before** anything but `/info` and `/pair`.
- **Host identity**: a self-signed certificate made once with `rcgen` on first listen. The certificate is in `identity.json` (§3.1); its private key is a Keychain item through the existing adapter (`adapters/keychain.rs`, service `com.sadburger.switchboard`) under the account `remote-key:<server_id>`, so two data directories under one macOS account never overwrite each other's keys. The bundle must be signed with the stable identity (`scripts/bundle.sh`) or the Keychain ACL is lost on every rebuild.
- **What the client pins** is the SPKI SHA-256 of the host's public key, not the certificate's bytes, so a certificate reissued from the same key (a new expiry) still verifies. Rotating the key is making a new identity: every pairing is invalid and the dialog says so.
- **Pairing verifies the key before the code is sent.** The code alone would let an intermediary terminate the first connection, forward the code to the real host, and take the token. So the pairing window shows a **QR code** carrying `{server_id, spki_sha256, code, addresses}`, and under it the same in text: a short form of the key hash and the code. The client scans or types both; it connects, compares the hash of the key it is actually talking to with the one it was given, and only when they match sends `/pair {code, device_name, spki_sha256}`. A client without a camera (visionOS gives an app none) pairs from the host's Bonjour record instead: it resolves the record, reads `/info` under no trust, shows the key the host presented in the dialog's short form for the owner to compare by eye, and pins that key for the pairing, so the typed code reaches only the host whose key the owner checked; a substituted certificate shows its own key on the device, where the owner sees it differ. The host refuses a pairing whose `spki_sha256` is not its own, so a relayed request through a substituted certificate fails even if the code reached it. Before pairing, `/info` is served to any client and nothing in it is trusted; after pairing, every connection verifies the pin before the token is presented.
- The pairing window is opened from the settings menu as "Allow pairing for 5 minutes", the same shape as the environment setup window (`ENV_SETUP_WINDOW`, never saved). The dialog that opens it chooses the scope the pairing grants, `read` by default.
- **The code**: eight characters from the 32-character Crockford alphabet (no `I`, `L`, `O`, `U`), 40 bits, drawn from the OS random source (`getrandom`), made when the window opens and shown as the QR's `code` and in text. It is single-use: the first successful `/pair` consumes it and closes the window. **Failures count globally**: one counter in the app's state, bumped on the frame for every failed `/pair` from any connection, and the window closes at three. Concurrent attempts cannot each get three, because the frame answers them in arrival order against the one counter.
- **The token**: 32 bytes from the OS random source, base64url, 43 characters. It does not expire; the owner revokes. It is sent only as a bearer header over the pinned connection, never in a URL.
- `/pair` answers with the token and the granted scope. The host stores the device name, scope, created time, last-seen time and the token's SHA-256 in `<data dir>/devices.json` (atomic write, owner-readable); never the token. The client stores the token and the pinned key hash in its Keychain.
- **Scope changes** happen in the host's dialog: a device's scope can be raised to `control` or lowered to `read` there, taking effect on the device's next request. There is no scope request over the port.
- **Key rotation** (a missing key at listen, §3.1) **deletes every record in `devices.json`** when the new identity is made, so an old token stops working on the first request, and the dialog says the pairings are gone. A client seeing a new key for a known `server_id` shows "identity changed, pair again" and sends nothing, token included.
- Every later request carries the bearer token; the host answers with the device's scope. A Settings dialog (built the way the Environment dialog is) lists paired devices with scope, last seen, and Revoke, and states what redaction does and does not cover. Revocation removes the record, takes effect on the next request and closes the device's WebSocket.

- Default view: all connected hosts, with source labels.
- Filter by server, working set, session kind, and state (`CardState` labels: waiting on you, working, idle, starting, exited, not running, not resumable).
- Sorting across hosts: the host's own rank (waiting first, then working, starting, idle, exited, not running, mirroring `CardState::rank`), then last activity, then record id as the tie-breaker.
- Server management screen: discovered and known servers, status, pairing, rename, enable/disable, forget.
- Working sets with the same name on different servers stay separate by qualified id; the UI groups by source.
- No client-made cross-host working set in v1. The host's sets are read-only from the client.

/// One HTTP request over a fresh pinned TLS connection: the status and
/// the body.
fn http(
    addr: SocketAddr,
    config: &Arc<ClientConfig>,
    method: &str,
    path: &str,
    bearer: Option<&str>,
    body: &str,
) -> std::io::Result<(u16, String)> {
    let tcp = TcpStream::connect(addr)?;
    tcp.set_read_timeout(Some(Duration::from_secs(10)))?;
    let conn = ClientConnection::new(
        Arc::clone(config),
        ServerName::try_from("localhost").unwrap(),
    )
    .map_err(std::io::Error::other)?;
    let mut s = StreamOwned::new(conn, tcp);
    while s.conn.is_handshaking() {
        s.conn.complete_io(&mut s.sock)?;
    }
    let auth = bearer
        .map(|t| format!("Authorization: Bearer {t}\r\n"))
        .unwrap_or_default();
    write!(
        s,
        "{method} {path} HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: localhost\r\n{auth}Content-Length: {}\r\n\r\n{body}",
        body.len()
    )?;
    s.flush()?;
    let mut reader = BufReader::new(s);
    let mut line = String::new();
    reader.read_line(&mut line)?;
    let status: u16 = line
        .split_whitespace()
        .nth(1)
        .and_then(|s| s.parse().ok())
        .ok_or_else(|| std::io::Error::new(std::io::ErrorKind::InvalidData, line.clone()))?;
    let mut length = 0usize;
    loop {
        let mut h = String::new();
        reader.read_line(&mut h)?;
        let h = h.trim_end();
        if h.is_empty() {
            break;
        }
        if let Some(v) = h.strip_prefix("Content-Length:") {
            length = v.trim().parse().unwrap_or(0);
        }
    }
    let mut out = vec![0; length];
    reader.read_exact(&mut out)?;
    Ok((status, String::from_utf8_lossy(&out).into_owned()))
}

content.content:
### 4.1 Implementation

- **No Tokio.** The host is std threads and `mpsc`; the core is owned by `SwitchboardApp` and every state change is a dispatch on the frame thread. The remote port follows the `ControlSocket` shape: an accept thread per listener, one thread per connection, each request handed over a channel to the frame, answered by the same `serve` path in `app.rs` (`serve_pending` runs before every frame, hidden ones included), the reply sent back on the connection's channel. A second runtime inside an egui app buys nothing for a handful of connections.
- **The frame does core state only.** A metadata request (a view, a command) is answered on the frame as the control port is. A content request (conversation, screen, run output, file) takes two steps: the frame answers with the **handle and the redaction policy** (the transcript path and resume handle, the pane's host id, the run's log path, the file's root and relative path, plus the secret values to mask and the policy fingerprint), and one **content worker thread** does the read, the parse, the mask, the version check and the serialization from a queue of such requests (one at a time, so one large parse is in memory at once; Spike 22 measured 575 MB peak for the largest transcript), then sends one small action back to the frame to record the version it observed (§4.4), and the connection thread writes the reply. The watch poll (§4.4) runs through the same worker. A multi-megabyte transcript, a 768 KiB file or a slow Keychain call therefore costs the worker its time and the asking connection its wait, never a frame. The handle is read under the frame's authority, so a record removed or rebound between the two steps makes the worker's version action a no-op and the reply carries the handle it read from.
- **Bounds.** The port is one user's few devices, and the limits say so:
  - at most 16 connections in total and 4 unauthenticated ones; a further accept is closed at once. The 4 are a separate pool: an unauthenticated flood fills its own slots and never a paired client's;
  - `/pair` is answered at most six times a minute per listener and `/info` sixty; past that the connection thread answers 429 without reaching the frame;
  - a TLS handshake and the first request line each within 5 s, a request body within 10 s, a write within 10 s; a connection that misses a deadline is closed;
  - one request in flight per connection (HTTP/1.1, no pipelining);
  - the frame drains at most 8 remote requests per pass, in arrival order, the rest waiting on the channel; the channel is bounded at 64 and a full channel answers 503 from the connection thread without reaching the frame; a frame-side request is a view or a handle lookup and takes microseconds, so the count is the bound;
  - each WebSocket subscriber has an event queue of 256; when it fills, the subscriber is sent `resync_required` and closed, never silently trimmed (§4.4);
  - the watch set (§4.4) is capped at 128 keys for the whole port; past the cap the least recently read key is evicted silently, since a read of an evicted key always works and re-enters it.
- Preferred crates: a blocking HTTP/1.1 server over `std::net::TcpListener` (hand-rolled or `tiny_http`), `tungstenite` for WebSocket, `rustls` with `rcgen` for the per-installation certificate, and `mdns-sd` (or the system `dns-sd` through a small macOS adapter) for Bonjour. All of it in `src/adapters/remote.rs` behind a `ports::remote` trait with a fake, and all of it must compile on Linux CI (Bonjour may be a `cfg(target_os = "macos")` adapter with a no-op elsewhere). **Spike 22 (§10) decides the exact crates before any of this is built.**
- Handlers are thin: HTTP request → auth and scope check → allowlist → `wire::Request` → `serve` → redaction → `wire::Reply` → HTTP response. No session or transcript logic lives in the adapter.
- Only the instance holding the store lock listens (as the control port does); a read-only instance refuses to bind.
- Bind to loopback by default until remote access is explicitly enabled in Settings. For LAN access, bind the chosen interface and require pairing.
- Configurable port in `identity.json` (§3.1), default `43187`, overridable with `SWITCHBOARD_REMOTE_PORT` (a dev aid, documented in the README) so two instances can run on one machine; `0` picks a free one, which the tests use.
- Advertise `_switchboard._tcp` via Bonjour only while listening on a non-loopback interface. TXT records carry the protocol major version (`v`), the display name (`name`) and the `server_id` (`id`, so a client matches a record to a known server before it connects); never a token, never key material. The instance name is the display name with a short id suffix, so two installations on one machine stay distinct.
- If Switchboard closes, the port goes away. A standalone daemon is not in scope.

### 4.2 API conventions
### 4.4 WebSocket events

Envelope:

```json
{
  "server_id": "uuid",
  "epoch": "uuid",
  "revision": 1042,
  "type": "changed",
  "resource": {"kind": "session", "id": "record-uuid"},
  "at_ms": 1760220000000
}
```

Event types:

- `hello {epoch, revision}`: the first frame on every subscription.
- **Scope.** A listing leaves out the records Dispatch made for its own use: a ticket's project with everything in it, and a worker session (the planner, an implementer, a reviewer) in any project, told by the `<ticket>-<nonce>` form of the op they were made under (`switchboard_control::is_dispatch_worker_op`). A supervisor's records (`sup-…`) and the owner's own are listed as ever, and a worker record is still read by its id, which is how the ticket view to come will reach them. `?scope=all` on `projects`, `sessions`, `waiting` and on the `events` subscription lists them and announces them; a plain subscription gets no `project`, `sessions`, `session` or `runs` frame about one. `info` lists `scope` among its capabilities. The point is the wire: hundreds of worker sessions on a host, which the headset fetched one project at a time, are now neither fetched nor announced.
- `changed {kind, id}` with the **metadata kinds** `project`, `space`, `set`, `session`; the **content kinds** `conversation`, `screen`, `run_output` (`id` = `record/n`), `file` (a pinned file, `id` = `project_id/path`); and the collection kinds `projects`, `spaces`, `sets` (with the space's id), `sessions` (with the project's id), `runs` (with the record's id), `waiting`, emitted when a collection's member id set moves and answered by refetching the collection whole; a global collection's `id` is the empty string. Each kind is its own resource key on the client (§4.2); a member fetched as part of its collection holds the collection's revision until it is read alone.
- `removed {kind, id}`: the resource is gone; the client drops it and marks any window on it "removed on <server>".
- `watching {kind, id}`: the answer to a `watch` frame (below).
- `resync_required`: sent before the host closes a subscriber whose queue overflowed; the client reconnects and refetches everything.

**What produces events.** The host has no event bus, and a save is not a reliable sign of a visible change: working sets save through `SaveViews`, Claude Code's trust question (`PromptSeen`) and a Codex pane going quiet (`HostListed`) change what a card says with no save at all. So the port does not watch for saves. Revision and events come from three places in `app.rs`:

1. **The read-model diff, after every pass.** After every `dispatch` and after every polling pass (`HostListed`, the hook log, `Tick`), the app recomputes a cheap per-resource fingerprint of each exported metadata read model (`SessionView`, `SetView` with its members, `ProjectView`, `SpaceView`, `waiting`) and compares it with the previous pass's. One `changed` per resource whose fingerprint moved, one `removed` per resource that vanished, one `changed` per collection whose membership moved, and `revision` bumped once per pass that emitted anything. The diff is the gate, not the effect list, so a set rename, a pin edit, a trust-question transition, a quiet-state transition and a time-based rule-set change all surface without anyone naming them. The fingerprint is a hash over the view's serialized bytes **with its time-derived fields held at zero**: `quiet_secs` is computed from the clock in `session_view` and would move every pass, so the view gains an additive `last_activity_ms` the client derives quiet from, and the quiet **state** (the card's word moving to idle) is what the diff sees. Collections carry the membership revision of §4.2, bumped only when the member id set moves. The hash is cheap at this scale (hundreds of records); the spike measures it (§10).
2. **Content versions, assigned where content is read.** Conversation text, pane text, run output and pinned files are mutable outside the core and can change between two reads inside one poll interval, so a content reply's revision cannot come from the counter alone. Every content read goes through a per-key **content cache** in `SwitchboardApp`, whose bookkeeping lives on the frame and whose reads run on the connection or worker thread (§4.1). The cache holds, per key, the **source version** and the **policy fingerprint of the owning project (§4.3)** it last served, with the revision it was assigned. The source version per kind, chosen so that no change the host can see leaves it unchanged:
   - **transcript**: size and mtime. Claude Code's JSONL only appends, Switchboard never edits one, and `/clear` or a discard rebinds the record to another file, so a growing size is a reliable version and a same-size rewrite does not occur;
   - **pinned file**: inode, ctime and size, read from the descriptor the walk ends on. No user tool preserves ctime, so an editor that rewrites in place, a same-size rewrite, and a replace-by-rename (a new inode) all move it;
   - **run output**: inode, ctime and size of the run's log. A log truncated and regrown to the same length has a new ctime; a rotated one a new inode;
   - **screen**: a hash of the pane text, as today.
   When either the source version or the policy fingerprint differs from what the cache holds, the worker's reply carries the new content and the frame, on the worker's version action, bumps `revision`, emits `changed {content kind, id}`, and stores the new version with that revision; the reply is stamped with that revision. **Two different content versions never share a revision for one key within an epoch**, and two reads of unchanged content return the same bytes and the same revision. The policy is resolved before the read; a resolution failure refuses the reply and leaves the cache untouched, so no earlier masked bytes stand in for the answer. A policy change is also noticed by the diff pass (the `env.*` actions are dispatches), which emits `changed` for every watched content key of the affected project without waiting for a read.
3. **The watch poll.** The port keeps a **watch set**: every content key any subscriber has asked to watch, plus every content key read in the last minute. Independently of the local view, every two seconds a worker thread checks each watched key's source version (a `stat`, or a pane snapshot for `screen`; never a parse) and, for a key that moved, reads it through the content cache, which is what emits the `changed`. The local session view reads its conversation through the same cache (an unmasked variant; §4.3), so the two polls share work rather than duplicate it. The set is capped at 128 keys (§4.1); past that the least recently read key is dropped, and a key with no subscriber and no read for a minute is dropped too. A read of a key not in the set still answers and still versions correctly, since the version is checked on every read; what eviction costs is the `changed` event until the next read, which the client's periodic refetch of a visible view covers.

**Watch frames.** A client sends `watch {kind, id}` when the first view instance on a content key opens and `unwatch` when the last one closes; the client keeps a reference count per key so closing one of two windows on a session changes nothing on the host. The host answers `watching` once the key is in its set, and the client fetches the initial content only after that, so the first snapshot's revision is covered by the poll from then on. A watch is never refused. On reconnect, after `hello`, the client resends every watch with a nonzero count before it snapshots. A visible content view also refetches on its own every thirty seconds, which is what covers a key the host evicted from the set.

**The conversation cache** moves from `UiState` to `SwitchboardApp` as one of the content caches, keyed by record id, resume handle and content version, read by the session view and the port alike; `UiState` keeps a reference, not a copy. This is a frontend change (the session, card and workflow views read the cache), so it is its own commit before any port code, Milestone A0 (§10), with the app behaving identically. This, the diff and the worker handoff are the changes to the app outside the adapter, and §12.6 says why they are required.

**Subscribe first, then snapshot.** A client connecting to a host:

1. opens the WebSocket and waits for `hello {epoch, revision}` (events start flowing at once and are buffered by the client);
2. fetches the snapshots it needs, each reply carrying its own `revision`;
3. applies the buffered events: an event whose `revision` is past a snapshot's `revision` invalidates that resource and is refetched; the rest were already in the snapshot;
4. enables commands.

Because the subscriber is registered on the frame thread before any later pass can bump `revision`, a metadata snapshot is taken on that thread with the revision it carries, and a content reply is stamped on that thread when the worker's version action lands (the same moment its `changed` would be emitted, so the event and the reply name one revision), no change can fall between a subscription and a snapshot. Several snapshots in flight are each reconciled against the buffer by their own revision; events that arrive during a refetch are reconciled the same way, which is why the client never clears its buffer until step 4. A resource named by an event the client has never seen is fetched. If `epoch` differs from the one the client holds (the host restarted), every cached item is stale and is refetched. There is no retained-event replay: a `resync_required` is the only answer to a gap, and events are never durable.

content.content:
### 4.1 Implementation

- **No Tokio.** The host is std threads and `mpsc`; the core is owned by `SwitchboardApp` and every state change is a dispatch on the frame thread. The remote port follows the `ControlSocket` shape: an accept thread per listener, one thread per connection, each request handed over a channel to the frame, answered by the same `serve` path in `app.rs` (`serve_pending` runs before every frame, hidden ones included), the reply sent back on the connection's channel. A second runtime inside an egui app buys nothing for a handful of connections.
- **The frame does core state only.** A metadata request (a view, a command) is answered on the frame as the control port is. A content request (conversation, screen, run output, file) takes two steps: the frame answers with the **handle and the redaction policy** (the transcript path and resume handle, the pane's host id, the run's log path, the file's root and relative path, plus the secret values to mask and the policy fingerprint), and one **content worker thread** does the read, the parse, the mask, the version check and the serialization from a queue of such requests (one at a time, so one large parse is in memory at once; Spike 22 measured 575 MB peak for the largest transcript), then sends one small action back to the frame to record the version it observed (§4.4), and the connection thread writes the reply. The watch poll (§4.4) runs through the same worker. A multi-megabyte transcript, a 768 KiB file or a slow Keychain call therefore costs the worker its time and the asking connection its wait, never a frame. The handle is read under the frame's authority, so a record removed or rebound between the two steps makes the worker's version action a no-op and the reply carries the handle it read from.
- **Bounds.** The port is one user's few devices, and the limits say so:
  - at most 16 connections in total and 4 unauthenticated ones; a further accept is closed at once. The 4 are a separate pool: an unauthenticated flood fills its own slots and never a paired client's;
  - `/pair` is answered at most six times a minute per listener and `/info` sixty; past that the connection thread answers 429 without reaching the frame;
  - a TLS handshake and the first request line each within 5 s, a request body within 10 s, a write within 10 s; a connection that misses a deadline is closed;
  - one request in flight per connection (HTTP/1.1, no pipelining);
  - the frame drains at most 8 remote requests per pass, in arrival order, the rest waiting on the channel; the channel is bounded at 64 and a full channel answers 503 from the connection thread without reaching the frame; a frame-side request is a view or a handle lookup and takes microseconds, so the count is the bound;
  - each WebSocket subscriber has an event queue of 256; when it fills, the subscriber is sent `resync_required` and closed, never silently trimmed (§4.4);
  - the watch set (§4.4) is capped at 128 keys for the whole port; past the cap the least recently read key is evicted silently, since a read of an evicted key always works and re-enters it.
- Preferred crates: a blocking HTTP/1.1 server over `std::net::TcpListener` (hand-rolled or `tiny_http`), `tungstenite` for WebSocket, `rustls` with `rcgen` for the per-installation certificate, and `mdns-sd` (or the system `dns-sd` through a small macOS adapter) for Bonjour. All of it in `src/adapters/remote.rs` behind a `ports::remote` trait with a fake, and all of it must compile on Linux CI (Bonjour may be a `cfg(target_os = "macos")` adapter with a no-op elsewhere). **Spike 22 (§10) decides the exact crates before any of this is built.**
- Handlers are thin: HTTP request → auth and scope check → allowlist → `wire::Request` → `serve` → redaction → `wire::Reply` → HTTP response. No session or transcript logic lives in the adapter.
- Only the instance holding the store lock listens (as the control port does); a read-only instance refuses to bind.
- Bind to loopback by default until remote access is explicitly enabled in Settings. For LAN access, bind the chosen interface and require pairing.
- Configurable port in `identity.json` (§3.1), default `43187`, overridable with `SWITCHBOARD_REMOTE_PORT` (a dev aid, documented in the README) so two instances can run on one machine; `0` picks a free one, which the tests use.
- Advertise `_switchboard._tcp` via Bonjour only while listening on a non-loopback interface. TXT records carry the protocol major version (`v`), the display name (`name`) and the `server_id` (`id`, so a client matches a record to a known server before it connects); never a token, never key material. The instance name is the display name with a short id suffix, so two installations on one machine stay distinct.
- If Switchboard closes, the port goes away. A standalone daemon is not in scope.

### 4.2 API conventions
### 4.4 WebSocket events

Envelope:

```json
{
  "server_id": "uuid",
  "epoch": "uuid",
  "revision": 1042,
  "type": "changed",
  "resource": {"kind": "session", "id": "record-uuid"},
  "at_ms": 1760220000000
}
```

Event types:

- `hello {epoch, revision}`: the first frame on every subscription.
- **Scope.** A listing leaves out the records Dispatch made for its own use: a ticket's project with everything in it, and a worker session (the planner, an implementer, a reviewer) in any project, told by the `<ticket>-<nonce>` form of the op they were made under (`switchboard_control::is_dispatch_worker_op`). A supervisor's records (`sup-…`) and the owner's own are listed as ever, and a worker record is still read by its id, which is how the ticket view to come will reach them. `?scope=all` on `projects`, `sessions`, `waiting` and on the `events` subscription lists them and announces them; a plain subscription gets no `project`, `sessions`, `session` or `runs` frame about one. `info` lists `scope` among its capabilities. The point is the wire: hundreds of worker sessions on a host, which the headset fetched one project at a time, are now neither fetched nor announced.
- `changed {kind, id}` with the **metadata kinds** `project`, `space`, `set`, `session`; the **content kinds** `conversation`, `screen`, `run_output` (`id` = `record/n`), `file` (a pinned file, `id` = `project_id/path`); and the collection kinds `projects`, `spaces`, `sets` (with the space's id), `sessions` (with the project's id), `runs` (with the record's id), `waiting`, emitted when a collection's member id set moves and answered by refetching the collection whole; a global collection's `id` is the empty string. Each kind is its own resource key on the client (§4.2); a member fetched as part of its collection holds the collection's revision until it is read alone.
- `removed {kind, id}`: the resource is gone; the client drops it and marks any window on it "removed on <server>".
- `watching {kind, id}`: the answer to a `watch` frame (below).
- `resync_required`: sent before the host closes a subscriber whose queue overflowed; the client reconnects and refetches everything.

**What produces events.** The host has no event bus, and a save is not a reliable sign of a visible change: working sets save through `SaveViews`, Claude Code's trust question (`PromptSeen`) and a Codex pane going quiet (`HostListed`) change what a card says with no save at all. So the port does not watch for saves. Revision and events come from three places in `app.rs`:

1. **The read-model diff, after every pass.** After every `dispatch` and after every polling pass (`HostListed`, the hook log, `Tick`), the app recomputes a cheap per-resource fingerprint of each exported metadata read model (`SessionView`, `SetView` with its members, `ProjectView`, `SpaceView`, `waiting`) and compares it with the previous pass's. One `changed` per resource whose fingerprint moved, one `removed` per resource that vanished, one `changed` per collection whose membership moved, and `revision` bumped once per pass that emitted anything. The diff is the gate, not the effect list, so a set rename, a pin edit, a trust-question transition, a quiet-state transition and a time-based rule-set change all surface without anyone naming them. The fingerprint is a hash over the view's serialized bytes **with its time-derived fields held at zero**: `quiet_secs` is computed from the clock in `session_view` and would move every pass, so the view gains an additive `last_activity_ms` the client derives quiet from, and the quiet **state** (the card's word moving to idle) is what the diff sees. Collections carry the membership revision of §4.2, bumped only when the member id set moves. The hash is cheap at this scale (hundreds of records); the spike measures it (§10).
2. **Content versions, assigned where content is read.** Conversation text, pane text, run output and pinned files are mutable outside the core and can change between two reads inside one poll interval, so a content reply's revision cannot come from the counter alone. Every content read goes through a per-key **content cache** in `SwitchboardApp`, whose bookkeeping lives on the frame and whose reads run on the connection or worker thread (§4.1). The cache holds, per key, the **source version** and the **policy fingerprint of the owning project (§4.3)** it last served, with the revision it was assigned. The source version per kind, chosen so that no change the host can see leaves it unchanged:
   - **transcript**: size and mtime. Claude Code's JSONL only appends, Switchboard never edits one, and `/clear` or a discard rebinds the record to another file, so a growing size is a reliable version and a same-size rewrite does not occur;
   - **pinned file**: inode, ctime and size, read from the descriptor the walk ends on. No user tool preserves ctime, so an editor that rewrites in place, a same-size rewrite, and a replace-by-rename (a new inode) all move it;
   - **run output**: inode, ctime and size of the run's log. A log truncated and regrown to the same length has a new ctime; a rotated one a new inode;
   - **screen**: a hash of the pane text, as today.
   When either the source version or the policy fingerprint differs from what the cache holds, the worker's reply carries the new content and the frame, on the worker's version action, bumps `revision`, emits `changed {content kind, id}`, and stores the new version with that revision; the reply is stamped with that revision. **Two different content versions never share a revision for one key within an epoch**, and two reads of unchanged content return the same bytes and the same revision. The policy is resolved before the read; a resolution failure refuses the reply and leaves the cache untouched, so no earlier masked bytes stand in for the answer. A policy change is also noticed by the diff pass (the `env.*` actions are dispatches), which emits `changed` for every watched content key of the affected project without waiting for a read.
3. **The watch poll.** The port keeps a **watch set**: every content key any subscriber has asked to watch, plus every content key read in the last minute. Independently of the local view, every two seconds a worker thread checks each watched key's source version (a `stat`, or a pane snapshot for `screen`; never a parse) and, for a key that moved, reads it through the content cache, which is what emits the `changed`. The local session view reads its conversation through the same cache (an unmasked variant; §4.3), so the two polls share work rather than duplicate it. The set is capped at 128 keys (§4.1); past that the least recently read key is dropped, and a key with no subscriber and no read for a minute is dropped too. A read of a key not in the set still answers and still versions correctly, since the version is checked on every read; what eviction costs is the `changed` event until the next read, which the client's periodic refetch of a visible view covers.

**Watch frames.** A client sends `watch {kind, id}` when the first view instance on a content key opens and `unwatch` when the last one closes; the client keeps a reference count per key so closing one of two windows on a session changes nothing on the host. The host answers `watching` once the key is in its set, and the client fetches the initial content only after that, so the first snapshot's revision is covered by the poll from then on. A watch is never refused. On reconnect, after `hello`, the client resends every watch with a nonzero count before it snapshots. A visible content view also refetches on its own every thirty seconds, which is what covers a key the host evicted from the set.

**The conversation cache** moves from `UiState` to `SwitchboardApp` as one of the content caches, keyed by record id, resume handle and content version, read by the session view and the port alike; `UiState` keeps a reference, not a copy. This is a frontend change (the session, card and workflow views read the cache), so it is its own commit before any port code, Milestone A0 (§10), with the app behaving identically. This, the diff and the worker handoff are the changes to the app outside the adapter, and §12.6 says why they are required.

**Subscribe first, then snapshot.** A client connecting to a host:

1. opens the WebSocket and waits for `hello {epoch, revision}` (events start flowing at once and are buffered by the client);
2. fetches the snapshots it needs, each reply carrying its own `revision`;
3. applies the buffered events: an event whose `revision` is past a snapshot's `revision` invalidates that resource and is refetched; the rest were already in the snapshot;
4. enables commands.

Because the subscriber is registered on the frame thread before any later pass can bump `revision`, a metadata snapshot is taken on that thread with the revision it carries, and a content reply is stamped on that thread when the worker's version action lands (the same moment its `changed` would be emitted, so the event and the reply name one revision), no change can fall between a subscription and a snapshot. Several snapshots in flight are each reconciled against the buffer by their own revision; events that arrive during a refetch are reconciled the same way, which is why the client never clears its buffer until step 4. A resource named by an event the client has never seen is fetched. If `epoch` differs from the one the client holds (the host restarted), every cached item is stale and is refetched. There is no retained-event replay: a `resync_required` is the only answer to a gap, and events are never durable.

input.content:
# Plan for #230: a browser page on the remote port, paired from a URL

References are to the worktree at 7fe8949 and were re-read there, not
copied from the notes. "Settled", "Unresolved" and "For the owner" are
the sections of the facts file. The page is built so that its basic
behaviour (pair, list, read, reply) does not depend on any Unresolved
line; where a line is Unresolved the decision says so.

## Where this departs from the issue

- **"The page opens `/api/v1/events` directly" and the token as a header.**
  `new WebSocket()` takes no headers (Settled, WHATWG), so the events
  socket carries the token as a subprotocol value, decision 2.
- **"The one-line excerpt the card shows" is not on the wire.** The spec
  (`docs/remote-client.md` §4.3) says the excerpt is `last_message` from
  the Stop hook "a field of the session's metadata". The hook event carries
  it (`src/ports/events.rs:24`) but nothing in `src/core` or `src/ports`
  stores it, and `SessionView` (`control/src/lib.rs:636-688`) has no such
  field (facts, Settled: tree). The plan adds no field. The page fetches
  `last-response` for the sessions it shows an excerpt for (below), as the
  headset does; an additive `SessionView.excerpt` is the later change if
  that costs too much, and it is the owner's call (For the owner 9).
- **"The device's scope in the header."** No reply after `/pair` carries
  it: `envelope` (`src/app.rs:3730-3741`) is epoch, revision, body, and
  `/info` is unauthenticated (`src/app.rs:3568-3600`). Spec §5 l.316,
  "the host answers with the device's scope", is not what the code does.
  The page shows the scope from the `/pair` reply and corrects itself on
  the first `403 scope` (`src/app.rs:3166-3172`), hiding the reply box. No
  endpoint is added (For the owner 8); the stale header is a known gap.
- **"Revoked said plainly."** Both refusals in `authenticate`
  (`src/app.rs:3125-3153`) are `401 unauthorized`, so the code cannot say
  revoked. The page does not need it: it holds a token, so a 401 means the
  host no longer knows the token, and it then reads `/info`: a different
  `spki_sha256` than the one it stored is "identity changed, pair again",
  the same key is "revoked". No new code (For the owner 7).
- **The `key` check does not defend the pairing the way §5 says.** Spec
  §5 (`docs/remote-client.md:309`) claims the host's `spki_sha256` check
  makes a relayed pairing fail. For a browser the body is built by
  whatever page the browser loaded, so under an impostor that check is
  fed by the impostor. What the page's comparison (URL `key` against
  `/info`) catches is a genuine page on the wrong genuine host: a second
  installation at that address or port, or a rotated key. The plan
  amends §5 to say so. The issue says roughly this already.
- **"Any path outside `/api/v1/` is refused"** holds (`src/app.rs:3023`),
  but after the request was queued to the frame. The static paths are
  answered before that, on the connection thread, so a page load costs the
  frame nothing (spec §4.1, "the frame does core state only").
- **"The browser then trusts that certificate for that address" is not
  safe to assume of this certificate.** `make_identity`
  (`src/adapters/remote.rs:95-127`) issues no subjectAltName, a CN only,
  and rcgen's year-4096 `not_after`. Apple's rule is a SAN and at most 825
  days; Chrome's is a SAN (Settled, HT210176 and the Chromium intent). Whether
  a no-SAN certificate can be clicked through on iOS is Unresolved. So the
  certificate is reissued with a SAN before any page is served (decision 1).
- **"Cookie versus subprotocol" leaves out where the token sits.** Neither
  option removes `localStorage`: a fetch from script needs the token in a
  header, and a cookie that `fetch` carries on its own rests on the
  Unresolved `SameSite`-on-WebSocket line. Decision 2 takes the path that
  does not.

## The record

One change, to `identity.json`; `devices.json`, `model.rs` and the workspace
records are untouched.

- **`Identity` gains two fields**, both `#[serde(default)]`
  (`src/ports/remote.rs:26-42`): `cert_names: Vec<String>`, the IP
  addresses and names the stored certificate carries as subjectAltName
  entries, and `cert_issued: Option<SystemTime>`. They exist so the host
  can tell a stale certificate without parsing DER (the adapter parses only
  the SPKI, `spki_sha256_of_cert`, `src/adapters/remote.rs:247`).
- **Version.** `IDENTITY_SCHEMA_VERSION` (`src/ports/remote.rs:17`, 1 today)
  becomes the value there at implementation time plus one, because a ticket
  landing in parallel may take the next number first. `SCHEMA_VERSION`
  (`src/core/model.rs:12`, 16 today) and `VIEWS_SCHEMA_VERSION` are not
  touched: nothing in `Workspace` or `Views` changes. `identity.json` has no
  `migrate` step (the identity is loaded by `load_identity`, `src/app.rs:2783`,
  not by `adapters::store::migrate`); an older file reads with an empty
  `cert_names`, which is "stale", which is the migration.
- **Rehydration.** Identity loads as today. At bind, and when a pairing
  window opens, a certificate whose `cert_names` lack the address
  `remote::local_address()` returns (`src/adapters/remote.rs:962-970`), or
  that is older than 400 days, is reissued over the **stored key**
  (`KeyPair::from_pem`, `src/adapters/remote.rs:138-140`; Settled, tree: the
  same `self_signed(&key)` call with a loaded key). `spki_sha256` does not
  move, so every native pin and every paired device holds (spec §5 l.308),
  and `devices.json` is not cleared, unlike the missing-key branch of
  `load_identity` (`src/app.rs:2806-2822`). The key stays Keychain-only.
- **The certificate is issued inside Apple's limits** so the unresolved
  "does the rule bind a user-trusted certificate" does not matter: SAN with
  the IP (and `<host>.local` when the machine's short name is known),
  `serverAuth` EKU, validity 800 days, P-256 as today.
- **On the device the page keeps** one `localStorage` entry:
  `{token, device_id, scope, spki_sha256, server_name}`. `localStorage` is
  per origin and script-readable (Settled, MDN); the CSP below allows no
  script but the page's own. The browser's own certificate exception is the
  browser's; the host keeps nothing per browser beyond the device record.
- **A browser is a `PairedDevice` like the others** (decision 6): the page
  sends a `device_name` made from `navigator.userAgent` ("Safari on
  iPhone"), which `new_device` cuts to 64 characters
  (`src/core/remote.rs:166-175`). No `kind` field; the name is enough.

## The signals

- **The URL.** `https://<host>:<port>/?code=<code>&key=<spki_sha256>&id=<server_id>`.
  The host is `local_address()`'s IP, bracketed when IPv6; every value is
  hex, Crockford or a UUID, so nothing needs escaping. The page's first
  statement reads `location.search` and calls `history.replaceState`
  (Settled, MDN: it rewrites the current history entry) before any
  request. Whether the code reaches history or iCloud tab sync before the
  script runs is Unresolved. The plan does not depend on it: the code is
  single-use and closes the window on `Paired`
  (`src/core/remote.rs:65-66`, Settled), and the failure counter closes it at
  three. The static replies carry `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer` so the
  `?code=` URL is not sent as a `Referer` to `/app.js`.
- **Pairing.** The page reads `/info`, refuses if `key` differs from
  `spki_sha256` (a `wrong_key` post would also count as one of the three
  failures, `src/app.rs:3639-3647`, so it never posts one), posts
  `/api/v1/pair {code, device_name, spki_sha256}`, stores the reply. With
  no code and no token the page shows how to open the window and a form for
  the typed code; it shows `/info`'s key in the dialog's short form for the
  owner to compare by eye, the headset's path (spec §5 l.309).
- **Token carrier.** `fetch` sends `Authorization: Bearer`. The socket
  offers `new WebSocket(url, ["switchboard.v1", "bearer.<token>"])`: both
  are `token` characters (Settled, RFC 6455 §4.1; a base64url token is
  `A-Za-z0-9-_`). The host echoes `switchboard.v1` and never the bearer
  value (Settled: only an offered value may be echoed, and the browser
  fails the handshake with none). A request with no subprotocol is the
  native client's and gets no echo. The token is taken from the
  `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` header **only on the upgrade to `events`**; on any
  other path only the `Authorization` header counts. The cookie route is not
  built: it rests on the Unresolved `SameSite` question. A device run that
  clears it makes a later change.
- **Cross-origin.** The host checks `Origin` (RFC 6455 §10.2, Settled) on the
  upgrade and on every non-GET: when `Origin` is present it must equal
  `https://<Host header>`, else `403 cross_origin`. This compares against
  the address the browser used, so it holds whichever allowlist the owner
  wants (IP, `.local`, loopback; For the owner 4). Native clients send no
  `Origin` and pass. No cookie is ambient, so this is a second line.
- **Live changes.** The page opens the socket, waits for `hello`, snapshots,
  then reconciles by revision (spec §4.4 "Subscribe first, then snapshot"):
  `waiting`, `projects`, each project's `sessions`; an event whose revision
  is past a snapshot's refetches that resource; a different `epoch`
  refetches everything. `resync_required` reconnects. It sends `watch` for
  the one open session's key (`conversation` or `screen`) and `unwatch` when
  it closes, so it holds one watch, not one per listed session, and does not
  press the 128-key cap (`src/app.rs:1789-1795`; whether many watches evict
  the headset's is the unmeasured one in For the owner 9, avoided).
- **Polling floor.** While the socket is down, or whenever it fails to
  open (a CSP `connect-src 'self'` that a browser does not match to `wss`,
  or a click-through that does not cover `wss`: both Unresolved), the page
  refetches `waiting` and the list every 10 s and says "live updates off".
  Acceptance does not depend on the socket.
- **Excerpts.** The list shows the card word, `waiting_reason` and the
  excerpt for waiting sessions and the first 16 listed, fetched from
  `last-response` unwatched, refetched when that session's `changed` arrives
  or on the 10 s tick.
- **Op ids** for `send` are 16 random bytes from `crypto.getRandomValues`
  in hex, not `randomUUID` (Settled: secure-context only; whether a
  bypassed page is one is Unresolved). A timed-out `send` is checked at
  `/ops/{op}` before it is repeated (spec §4.5).
- **States said plainly.** "Identity changed, pair again" and "revoked" as
  above; "this device reads only" when `scope` was refused; "the host did
  not answer" otherwise.

  the frame, in `connection` (`src/adapters/remote.rs`): `GET /` (and the

  The three files are `web/index.html`, `web/app.js`, `web/app.css`, held
  as `include_str!` constants in a new `src/adapters/web.rs`. Content types
  `text/html; charset=utf-8`, `text/javascript; charset=utf-8`,
  `text/css; charset=utf-8`. Every static reply carries
  `Cache-Control: no-store`, `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`,
  `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer` and
